prompt: Why didn't Harvard have calculus classes when it first opened?
answer:
Harvard did not offer calculus when it opened because the subject, in its modern form, had not yet been developed. Harvard was founded in 1636, while Newton and Leibniz developed systematic differential and integral calculus in the late 17th century—roughly the 1660s–1680s.

Harvard did teach mathematics from at least 1638, mainly the subjects then considered appropriate in a classical college curriculum, such as arithmetic, algebra, geometry, astronomy, and classical natural philosophy. Instruction in higher mathematics, including calculus, was established later, during the 18th century.  

Strictly speaking, earlier mathematicians—including Archimedes and medieval scholars—had developed important ideas resembling parts of calculus, so saying that calculus “had not been invented” is a convenient simplification.
